newsitem.title: USA: Rich nations extend debt relief for poor countries.
newsitem.headline: Rich nations extend debt relief for poor countries.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
Wealthy creditor nations agreed on Saturday to sharply increase the assistance they are prepared to give to the world's poorest debtor countries in a multibillion-dollar international plan.
Under the new initiative, up to 80 percent of their debts would be forgiven, compared with a 67 percent ceiling now.

The debt-relief initiative -- involving actions by the Paris Club of creditor countries, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank -- is aimed at putting debt-ridden poor nations, many of them in Africa, back on their feet.
Uganda is expected to be the first country to benefit from the plan.
"I hope we will be able to have the first countries to benefit from (the initiative)...before the end of the year," Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said.

"We can all be satisfied that finance will be forthcoming ...one way or the other," Clarke told reporters after a meeting of finance ministers and central bankers of the Group of Seven richest industrial nations.

G7 endorsement of the expanded debt relief paves the way for the formal launch of the multilateral debt relief plan during the current annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank that ends on October 3.
The G7 comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States, main players of the Paris Club.

Both the World Bank and the IMF had urged the Paris Club of creditor nations to expand their debt relief to cover up to 90 percent of their loans to eligible poor nations. But the G7, which forms the backbone of the Club, baulked.
According to some estimates, about four or five countries will not be able to put their economies back on even keel with only 80 percent forgiveness of their Paris Club debt.
The IMF and World Bank would have to cover the difference to ensure that did not happen. The balance at issue amounts to some $1.2 billion.
The World Bank has already pledged $2 billion to the initiative.
The IMF board last week pledged to come up with the necessary financing to take part in the debt relief plan, but left open the question of where the money would come from.

Britain, the U.S. and some other countries have urged the IMF to sell some of its nearly 104 million ounces of gold to finance its participation in the programme until a permanent and self-financing facility can be be put in place.
But Italy, and especially Germany, are opposed and instead want the IMF to rely on bilateral contributions from its member nations to finance stepped-up aid to poor countries.
Clarke did not say whether the discussions touched on methods of financing other than the controversial gold sales.
